description_full: Flowers Foods, Inc. produces and markets packaged bakery food products in the United States. The company's principal products include fresh breads, buns, rolls, snack items, bagels, English muffins, tortillas, baking mixes, and frozen breads and rolls as well as snack items including bars, cakes, cookies, and crackers. The company offers its products under the Nature's Own, DKB, Canyon Bakehouse, Simple Mills, Wonder, and Tastykake brand names. It distributes its products through a direct-store-delivery distribution and a warehouse delivery system, as well as operates bakeries. The company's customers include national and regional restaurants, institutions and foodservice distributors, and retail in-store bakeries; wholesale distributors; mass merchandisers, supermarkets, vending outlets, and convenience stores; quick-serve chains, food wholesalers, institutions, dollar stores, and vending companies; and public health care, military commissaries, and prisons, and other governmental institutions. The company was formerly known as Flowers Industries and changed its name to Flowers Foods, Inc. in 2001. Flowers Foods, Inc. was founded in 1919 and is headquartered in Thomasville, Georgia.

financial_summary: Flowers Foods, Inc. is a small-cap consumer defensive business with a $1.4B market cap on $5.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +3% over the past three years and +3% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 11% against a 6% cost of capital, a 5-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $319M in free cash flow — roughly 6 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 5.32× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -8.7% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 5.1× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 2.3× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 15.1% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 8.0% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.4× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.
